A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DHSA, with readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained content can be matched despite the changed title and substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original Needle-in-a-Haystack and LongBench evaluations, alongside latency, memory, and KV-cache analyses in its main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and RULER results, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and GPU/CPU performance measurements.

M1.justification: The reported execution procedure changes from explicit token-level similarity/mask construction in v1 to compact, budgeted key-index routing in v2. v2 adds tiled online-softmax execution alongside SDPA and replaces the explicit decode algorithm with a prefill-focused workflow using dense decoding in evaluation. The boundary predictor, soft-label loss, and square-root length normalization remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 expands the reported LongBench coverage from 11 datasets to 16, adding TREC, PassageCount, PassageRetrieval_en, LCC, and RepoBench-P, including synthetic and code tasks absent from v1's results. It also adds RULER, including distributed-information tasks QA-1, QA-2, and VT. The three boundary-predictor training datasets are retained.

E2.justification: The LongBench comparison expands beyond dense and Block Sparse attention to StreamingLLM and its variants, MInference, DuoAttention, SeerAttention, and Quest, with model-specific participation documented in v2 Table 1. StreamingLLM previously appeared only in supplementary comparisons. The earlier H2O and PyramidKV performance comparisons disappear. Block Sparse remains the same comparator despite its changed citation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces LLaMA and Qwen configurations, including 4-bit and BF16 evaluations, CPU measurements, and batch-size experiments. Fixed token budgets are replaced by density-based settings of 6.25%, 12.5%, and 25%; LongBench's Block Sparse block size changes from 256 to 128. Needle retrieval extends to much longer contexts, and new evaluations distinguish attention-kernel latency from end-to-end TTFT. These changes prevent direct cross-version performance comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate component-removal ablations in Table 4, systematic boundary-window and NMS sensitivity tests in Table 7, attention-recovery analyses, and routing-overhead breakdowns. Budget analysis expands into LongBench density sweeps. Conversely, v1's boundary-sharing variant and supplementary KV-capacity/generated-length sensitivity studies are removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 2 introduces shaded bands around recall curves, absent from v1's plots, but neither its caption nor the text defines their statistical meaning. Neither PDF specifies seeds, repeated-run counts, or confidence-interval procedures. Whether the new bands represent uncertainty estimates or another form of variation therefore remains unresolved.

E6.justification: v2 replaces or expands much of the reported result set under different models, budgets, and aggregation. New LLaMA LongBench averages are 31.8 for DHSA, 27.9 for Block Sparse, and 32.7 for dense attention (Table 1); corresponding 48K RULER scores are 71.5, 43.1, and 75.2 (Table 5). Table 9 adds average TTFT of 1.88 seconds versus 3.28 for dense FA2. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v1 contains method equations and a short complexity discussion but no comparable recall theory. v2 Appendix B adds semantic-segment and boundary-accuracy assumptions, a chunk-score stability lemma, and conditional recall bounds with proofs for DHSA and fixed block sparsity. It also expands the complexity analysis to account for chunk similarity and routing.

C1.justification: The central dynamic-chunking idea persists, but v2 adds explicit model/hardware portability and long-context feasibility claims: GPU/CPU support, 100K-context LLaMA inference on a 24GB GPU, and up to 10× prefill speedup at 128K. These replace v1's emphasis on on-device Gemma inference, percentage memory reductions, and applicability to both prefill and decoding.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits its target to prefill-dominated workloads and defers decoding optimization. It adds interpretations of distributed-evidence preservation, routing-overhead tradeoffs, sequential batching under memory constraints, and window-size sensitivity. v1's discussion of unsuccessful Gemma context extension and future adaptive budget allocation is removed rather than relocated.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents separate predictor training per backbone, 10,000 training steps and approximately 8.89 hours for Gemma, detailed baseline allocations, CPU hardware/software, 128-token row/column tiles, and buffer/routing reuse. Algorithms 1–3 substantially expand execution details. These disclosures improve reproducibility; the newly stated training duration does not establish a changed training budget. The repository link is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial Related Work section positioning DHSA among sparse attention, alternative long-context architectures, and memory-constrained inference systems. New references include DuoAttention, SeerAttention, Quest, FlashAttention, state-space models, quantization, and speculative decoding. Publication updates to retained works such as LongBench and StreamingLLM are bibliographic changes rather than new research relationships.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 adds a motivation section, separates inference acceleration from the core method, and introduces dedicated related work. Much of v1 Appendix B survives in reorganized Appendix A subsections, while workflow material is redistributed and the standalone limitations section disappears.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column presentation. The framework diagram is redrawn around index routing, the boundary-predictor diagram moves into the main text, and LongBench tables change from individual-dataset columns to task-category panels across models. New recall, density, CPU, batching, and ablation displays replace much of the earlier memory/decoding presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for DHSA's practical prefill benefits. Component ablations address v1's limited isolation of the proposed mechanisms, RULER tests distributed evidence beyond needle retrieval, and broader baseline comparisons plus end-to-end TTFT/overhead measurements make the efficiency claims more assessable. Backend algorithms and calibration details also improve reproducibility. Explicit peak-memory and decoding studies are lost, and the new shaded bands remain unexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and technical clarity.
